events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Battle of Gettysburg Begins
events.blurb: Confederate soldiers advancing through a Pennsylvania town accidentally encountered Union cavalry, triggering three days of fighting that became the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. A total of approximately 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, or went missing — roughly one in three of all combatants engaged on both sides.

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: Scopes "Monkey Trial" Begins
events.blurb: John T. Scopes, a high school teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, went on trial for violating a state law banning the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The case — which pitted famed defense attorney Clarence Darrow against three-time presidential nominee and Christian fundamentalist William Jennings Bryan — was broadcast nationally on radio and drew journalists from across the country to the small town.
events.revealBlurb: July 10, 1925 — Dayton, Tennessee. The trial was deliberately staged by the town's businessmen to attract tourists and publicity; Scopes wasn't sure he had actually taught evolution. He was convicted and fined $100, but the verdict was overturned on a technicality. Bryan died five days after the trial ended.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes
events.blurb: A 29-year-old women's tennis champion beat a 55-year-old former men's Wimbledon champion in straight sets at a televised exhibition match at a Houston indoor arena, before 30,000 spectators and an estimated 90 million television viewers worldwide. The older player had spent months mocking women's tennis in the press; he entered the arena on a rickshaw pulled by models in skimpy outfits and gave her a Sugar Daddy lollipop at the net.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1973 — Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 at the Houston Astrodome. King had threatened to boycott the US Open unless prize money was equal; Forest Hills agreed in time for the tournament that August — the first Slam to do so.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Sally Ride in Space
events.blurb: A 32-year-old astrophysicist, riding as mission specialist aboard a space shuttle launched from a Florida coastal site, became the first American woman — and the youngest American — to reach orbit. NASA had asked her at the pre-flight press conference whether space travel would affect her reproductive organs; she answered that there was no evidence either way.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — Space Shuttle Challenger, STS-7 mission. She flew a second mission in 1984 and was on the commission investigating the 1986 Challenger disaster that killed seven of her colleagues. She came out as a lesbian in her 2012 obituary.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: Back to the Future Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old director released a 116-minute time-travel comedy about a teenager who accidentally travels 30 years into his own past and must ensure his parents fall in love so he himself will exist. The original cast had been halfway through shooting with a different lead actor when the director fired him and reshot the entire film with a new star. The resulting product became the top-grossing film of its year and spawned two sequels.
events.revealBlurb: July 3, 1985 — Robert Zemeckis, starring Michael J. Fox and Christopher Lloyd. The original Marty was Eric Stoltz; replacing him cost $4 million in reshoots. The DeLorean was Zemeckis's choice — he wanted a time machine that looked, plausibly, like a spaceship.

events.title: Pulp Fiction Released
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American director released a 154-minute crime picture with a deliberately non-linear structure, three loosely interwoven storylines, and dialogue about hamburgers, foot massages, and divine intervention. It had cost $8 million, been passed on by multiple studios, and been rescued by a new boutique distributor. It won the top prize at Cannes, grossed over $200 million, and pulled a whole generation of independent filmmakers into its wake.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1994 — Quentin Tarantino, released by Miramax. The opening Cannes screening received a 15-minute standing ovation. John Travolta's comeback, the soundtrack's surf-rock revival, and the dance scene became instant cultural touchstones.

events.title: Alice in Wonderland Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Oxford mathematics don who had developed a story three years earlier during a boating trip with three little girls, the daughter of the dean of his college, published a book-length expansion of it. The nonsense-logic adventures of a curious girl falling into a subterranean world of mad tea parties, playing-card royalty, and cat grins without cats became the foundation text of modern children's literature.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1865 — Charles Dodgson, pen name Lewis Carroll. Alice Liddell was the model; their rowboat trip on July 4, 1862 was three years earlier to the day. The 1862 handwritten original, illustrated by Carroll, was given to Alice; it is now in the British Library.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Elvis's First Sun Session
events.blurb: A 19-year-old truck driver who had walked into a small Memphis recording studio a year earlier to make an acetate for his mother's birthday showed up for a late-night try-out with two local session musicians. The session was going nowhere until, during a break, the kid started goofing around with an old R&B song by Arthur Crudup. The engineer slapped the tape on and caught it. Within weeks the song was a regional hit.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1954 — Elvis Presley, Scotty Moore, and Bill Black at Sun Records, Memphis. The song was "That's All Right (Mama)." Studio owner Sam Phillips had famously said he could make "a billion dollars" if he could find a white man who sang with a Black feel.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: Harvey Publishes De Motu Cordis
events.blurb: A 50-year-old English royal physician published a 72-page Latin treatise correctly describing, for the first time, the circulation of the blood — with the heart as a muscular pump, arteries carrying blood outward, veins returning it, and the two sides of the heart circulating distinct streams between the body and the lungs. He had been working on the theory for nearly two decades and had presented earlier versions in lectures. The medical establishment largely ignored the book for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: 1628 — William Harvey, "Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus." Harvey's practice lost patients initially as word spread of his heresy. He lived long enough to see the theory accepted; he died in 1657 at 79, still personally treating King Charles II.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
events.blurb: A 62-year-old French chemist, who had been working for years on vaccines against animal diseases, administered his experimental rabies vaccine — desiccated spinal cord tissue from infected rabbits — to a 9-year-old Alsatian boy who had been savaged by a rabid dog two days earlier. The boy received 13 injections over ten days and survived. Rabies, previously universally fatal once symptoms appeared, now had an effective post-exposure prophylaxis.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1885 — Louis Pasteur; patient was Joseph Meister. Pasteur was not licensed as a physician; he could have been prosecuted if the boy had died. Meister grew up, became the gatekeeper at the Institut Pasteur, and is said to have killed himself in 1940 rather than let Nazi troops enter Pasteur's tomb (disputed; he may have died from gas poisoning unrelated).

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Salk Polio Vaccine
events.blurb: The University of Michigan School of Public Health announced that the 40-year-old Pittsburgh virologist's killed-virus polio vaccine — tested the previous year on 1.8 million children in the largest medical trial then conducted — was "safe, effective, and potent." Polio, which had paralyzed 57,000 American children in 1952, became a preventable disease overnight. Millions wept in the streets. The vaccine's developer was offered a patent; he famously refused.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1955 — Jonas Salk. Edward R. Murrow asked him who owned the patent; he answered: "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" The Sabin oral vaccine, using live attenuated virus, arrived 1961 and became the standard globally.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Sojourner Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: Mars Pathfinder landed on the Ares Vallis flood plain using airbag cushioning, bouncing 15 times before rolling to a stop, and deployed a 10.5 kg six-wheeled rover named Sojourner — the first wheeled vehicle to operate on another planet. Over 83 Martian days the rover analyzed the chemical composition of 16 rock targets, including samples scientists nicknamed Barnacle Bill and Yogi.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1997 — Mars Pathfinder. Sojourner was designed for a 7-sol mission and lasted 83. It could fit on a kitchen counter. Mission scientists named rocks after cartoon and pop-culture characters; one rock was called "Casper" because it appeared strangely bright. The rover traveled just 100 meters total — less than a city block.

events.title: Perseverance Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater — a 45 km ancient river delta — using the same sky-crane system as Curiosity but upgraded with a terrain-relative navigation system that steered around boulders autonomously during descent. The mission carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which made the first powered flight on another planet six weeks after landing.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 2021 — Mars 2020. Perseverance carries 43 sealed titanium tubes designed to cache Martian rock samples for a future return mission — a plan with no confirmed launch date but an estimated $10 billion price tag. It also produced breathable oxygen from the Martian atmosphere using an instrument called MOXIE, demonstrating a technology critical for crewed Mars missions.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Patented
events.blurb: A textile worker patented a multi-spindle spinning frame that allowed a single operator to spin eight threads simultaneously — a number later increased to 120. The machine slashed the cost of cotton yarn and displaced the hand-spinning cottage industry within a generation.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Homestead Strike
events.blurb: A Pennsylvania steelworkers' strike against wage cuts at a mill owned by a famous industrialist turned into a gun battle after management hired 300 Pinkerton private detectives to escort strike-breakers into the plant. The Pinkertons arrived by barge up the Monongahela River before dawn; strikers and their families met them on the banks with rifles. Nine strikers and seven Pinkertons died in the all-day firefight. The state militia restored order; the union was broken; US steelworkers remained largely non-unionized for 45 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1892 — Homestead Steel Works, owned by Andrew Carnegie, managed during the strike by Henry Clay Frick. Frick survived an assassination attempt by anarchist Alexander Berkman three weeks later, shot and stabbed multiple times but recovered. Carnegie was in Scotland when the violence occurred.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Rembrandt's Night Watch
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter completed a 3.6 by 4.4 metre group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company, commissioned by 18 civic-guard officers each paying 100 guilders for his place. Unlike the static lineup portraits typical of the genre, the painter depicted the company in motion, emerging from a shadowed arch with a drum rolling and a musket firing. The title "Night Watch" is a misnomer added by 19th-century curators; varnish had darkened a daytime scene.
events.revealBlurb: 1642 — Rembrandt van Rijn. Now in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. It was trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit between two doorways, losing two figures. A recent 8K restoration reconstructed the missing pieces using AI.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Goya's Third of May 1808
events.blurb: A Spanish court painter in his late sixties completed a large canvas commemorating the execution of Spanish civilians by French occupying troops six years earlier. A man in a white shirt stretches his arms out cruciform, illuminated by a lantern at ground level; the executioners are faceless soldiers. The painting broke with the flattering conventions of history painting, depicting the victims as ordinary and terrified rather than heroic. Its brutality shocked its first audiences.
events.revealBlurb: 1814 — Francisco Goya. Commissioned, remarkably, by the restored Spanish monarch who the French had deposed — Ferdinand VII. Now in Madrid's Prado. It directly influenced Manet's Execution of Maximilian and Picasso's Guernica.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Battle of Britain
events.blurb: For nearly four months, an island nation's outnumbered fighter force faced daily mass raids by the world's most battle-hardened air force, with the explicit goal of destroying aerial defences so that a seaborne invasion could follow. Radar stations, sector control rooms, and the pilots' ability to keep flying became the three fulcrums on which the outcome balanced.
events.revealBlurb: July 10 – October 31, 1940. The RAF lost 1,023 aircraft; the Luftwaffe lost 1,887. Churchill's "The Few" speech on August 20 honoured the pilots — the average age of whom was just 20. Germany quietly postponed its invasion plan on September 17 and never rescheduled it.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Battle of Kursk
events.blurb: Two million soldiers and nearly 6,000 tanks clashed around a salient in the steppe, with the attackers driving into prepared defences twelve layers deep that had been built specifically to absorb and exhaust an armoured offensive. For the first time in the eastern conflict, a major German armoured attack was stopped before achieving a breakthrough.
events.revealBlurb: July 5 – August 23, 1943. The Germans had repeatedly delayed the offensive to wait for newer tanks, giving Soviet intelligence — fed by the British Ultra intercepts — five months to prepare. The opening day, July 5, was the single costliest day in the history of aerial warfare by aircraft lost. Germany never regained strategic initiative in the East afterward.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Great Schism of Christianity
events.blurb: The pope's legate and the patriarch of a Bosphorus capital excommunicated each other over a long-brewing dispute about papal authority, the phrasing of the Nicene Creed, and the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist. Mutual anathemas remained in force for 911 years. The Roman and Orthodox churches have never fully reunited.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1054 — Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius. The excommunications were formally lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras. The "filioque clause" dispute sounds obscure but was genuinely the trigger.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Botticelli's Primavera
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a large poplar panel for the bedroom of a Medici cousin, depicting nine mythological figures in a grove of orange trees — Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, a gusting wind god chasing a nymph who is transformed into the flower-bearing goddess of spring. It is among the first Renaissance paintings to take mythological (not religious) subject matter on its own terms.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1482 — Sandro Botticelli. The painting contains at least 500 identifiable plant species, some 190 different flowers. Botticelli was later nearly destroyed by Savonarola's movement and reportedly burned some of his own work in the bonfire of the vanities.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Picasso's Guernica
events.blurb: A Spanish painter in his mid-fifties produced a 3.5-metre-tall monochrome canvas for the Spanish pavilion at a Paris international exposition, depicting the destruction of a Basque town by Nazi and Fascist bombers at the request of the Spanish Nationalist forces a month earlier. Screaming women, a dismembered soldier, a wounded horse, a bull, and a single lightbulb-like eye crowd the picture. The artist refused to have it displayed in his homeland until fascist rule there ended.
events.revealBlurb: Painted January-June 1937; exhibited July 12 at the Paris Exhibition. Picasso. The bombing of Guernica was on April 26, 1937. The painting toured the world for 40 years, then was installed in Madrid in 1981, six years after Franco's death.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: Elvis Presley Dies
events.blurb: A 42-year-old singer was found unresponsive on a bathroom floor of his Memphis mansion in the early afternoon and pronounced dead at a local hospital an hour later. The cause was heart failure, probably exacerbated by a cocktail of barbiturates prescribed by his personal physician. 80,000 mourners lined the four-kilometre route to the cemetery; his face had appeared on 150 magazine covers in his lifetime and would appear on tens of thousands more after his death.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1977 — Elvis Presley at Graceland, Memphis. An autopsy found 14 different drugs in his system. His doctor, George Nichopoulos, had his license revoked years later. "Elvis sightings" began the day after the funeral and have never entirely stopped.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Mexican Independence
events.blurb: An 11-year war that had begun with a village priest ringing his church bell ended when a former royalist colonel, having switched sides and joined forces with an insurgent guerilla, marched his Army of the Three Guarantees into Mexico City. A Spanish viceroy signed the Treaty of Córdoba recognizing Mexican independence. The new country was briefly a monarchy, then a republic; it would lose over half its territory to the United States within three decades.
events.revealBlurb: September 27, 1821 — Agustín de Iturbide entered Mexico City. The war had begun September 16, 1810; Iturbide had earlier been on the royalist side, defeating the revolutionary José María Morelos. Mexico's Independence Day remains September 16 (the "Grito"), not the 27th.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Gangnam Style Goes Viral
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper was uploaded to YouTube, featuring a catchy synth-pop track, exaggerated dance moves, and satirical shots of an upscale Seoul district. Within three months the video had 300 million views, passing Justin Bieber's "Baby" as the most-viewed in YouTube history. Within five, it crossed one billion. The horse-riding dance broke through into American late-night comedy, political campaigns, and every wedding reception in the world.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2012 — PSY (Park Jae-sang). It held the most-viewed YouTube video title until it was surpassed by "See You Again" in 2017 and then "Despacito." The video's 2014 view count literally broke YouTube's 32-bit counter, requiring an engineering upgrade to 64 bits.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Stranger Things Premieres
events.blurb: A supernatural drama set in a small Indiana town in 1983 premiered on Netflix, combining Spielbergian child adventure, Stephen King atmospheric horror, and 80s-movie production design with a pitch-perfect synth-wave score. The 8-episode first season was Netflix's first genuine original-production cultural sensation and proved that the streaming service could create prestige-TV hits without a traditional network. The cast of unknown child actors became overnight celebrities.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2016 — Netflix; created by the Duffer Brothers. Cast included Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Noah Schnapp. The 2022 season 4 episode "Running Up That Hill" pushed Kate Bush's 1985 single to #1 in the UK, 37 years after its original release.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Battle of the Golden Spurs
events.blurb: A militia army of Flemish townsmen and weavers, defending a swampy battlefield outside a cloth-making city, slaughtered an elite French feudal cavalry force whose horses bogged down charging across the ditches the Flemings had dug. Five hundred gilded spurs were collected from the dead knights and hung in a nearby church, giving the battle its name. It was an early hint that trained infantry could defeat mounted nobility.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1302 — Courtrai (Kortrijk). The defeat shocked French chivalry and triggered a long reform of French military organization. July 11 is still celebrated as the official holiday of the Flemish Community of Belgium.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Founding of Rome
events.blurb: According to Roman tradition, Romulus killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city's walls, then became the first king of a settlement of seven hills beside the Tiber. Varro, working backward from consular lists, calculated the exact date centuries later and Rome adopted it as its birthday, celebrating it annually with the Parilia festival.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 753 BCE — the traditional date. Romulus allegedly populated his new city by opening it as a sanctuary for fugitives, runaway slaves, and exiles. When women were in short supply, he invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and had his men abduct their daughters.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.blurb: A fire that broke out near the Circus Maximus burned for nine days and destroyed or severely damaged ten of Rome's fourteen districts, leaving the majority of the population homeless. Emperor Nero, who was at Antium when the fire started, blamed the city's small Christian community and launched the first state-sanctioned persecution of Christians in Roman history.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 64 CE. The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is almost certainly false — the fiddle didn't exist yet, and multiple sources place him outside the city at the time. Tacitus, writing fifty years later, noted that many Romans suspected Nero ordered the fire himself but that the charge was never proven.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Bank Nationalization
events.blurb: The prime minister, locked in a bitter succession battle with her party's old guard, issued an overnight ordinance nationalizing 14 of India's largest private commercial banks, which between them held 70 percent of national deposits. The move was enormously popular; it redirected credit from urban industrialists toward rural farmers and small businesses, and left her party's conservative faction looking like bankers' men. It cemented her political dominance.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1969 — Indira Gandhi. The Supreme Court overturned the ordinance; she re-issued it as legislation. Her left-populist turn fractured the Congress party. Insurance companies were nationalized two years later.

events.title: Smiling Buddha Nuclear Test
events.blurb: Scientists detonated a plutonium-implosion device in a shaft drilled beneath a Rajasthani desert, giving India membership in an exclusive club of nuclear-weapon states. The government described the test as a "peaceful nuclear explosion," a distinction the international community did not accept. Canada and the United States, which had supplied the research reactor whose plutonium fueled the device, were furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1974 — on Buddha Jayanti, the Buddha's birthday. Project director Raja Ramanna telephoned Indira Gandhi: "The Buddha is smiling." The device yielded 8-12 kilotons, not the 12-15 initially claimed.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Narendra Modi Elected PM
events.blurb: A three-term chief minister of a western state led his party to the first single-party majority in an Indian general election in 30 years, campaigning on development, anti-corruption, and Hindu-nationalist themes after ten years of a Congress-led coalition. The ruling party was reduced to 44 seats, its worst defeat since independence. The new prime minister was sworn in at a ceremony attended by leaders from across South Asia.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 2014 — results declared; Modi sworn in May 26. The BJP won 282 of 543 seats. Modi had been denied a U.S. visa for years over the 2002 Gujarat riots; that travel ban was lifted on his election.

events.title: Trinity Nuclear Test
events.blurb: A plutonium implosion device was detonated atop a 30-metre steel tower in the New Mexico desert, producing a fireball visible 160 kilometres away and an explosion equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Watching from a bunker 16 kilometres distant, the project's scientific director later recalled a verse from Hindu scripture about becoming death, destroyer of worlds.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: U-2 Incident
events.blurb: A high-altitude American reconnaissance aircraft was shot down deep inside Soviet territory by a surface-to-air missile. The CIA assumed the pilot was dead and issued a cover story about a weather research flight gone astray. Then Khrushchev triumphantly produced the pilot alive and the wreckage intact, humiliating the U.S. president on the eve of a Paris summit.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1960 — pilot Francis Gary Powers ejected over Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg). He was traded two years later for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge — the same swap dramatized in "Bridge of Spies."

events.title: Partial Test Ban Treaty
events.blurb: Three nuclear powers signed a treaty in Moscow banning atmospheric, underwater, and outer-space testing of nuclear weapons — while carefully preserving their right to test underground. The agreement was driven partly by rising public alarm over radioactive fallout, which scientists had detected in the teeth of American children born far from any test site.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1963 — signed by the US, UK, and USSR. France and China, who weren't invited, kept atmospheric testing for years. Strontium-90 levels in baby teeth dropped sharply within a decade.

events.title: Moscow Olympics Boycott
events.blurb: Sixty-six nations, led by the United States, refused to send athletes to the Summer Games held in the Soviet capital, protesting the invasion of a neighboring country five months earlier. Eighty nations competed anyway — the smallest field since 1956. Four years later, the Soviet bloc returned the favor by boycotting the Los Angeles Games.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1980 — the boycott was announced by Jimmy Carter. British athletes defied their own government and competed under the Olympic flag. The 1984 Soviet retaliation cost American sprinter Evelyn Ashford a likely gold-medal duel.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: Apollo–Soyuz Handshake in Space
events.blurb: An American Apollo Command Module and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked 225 km above the Atlantic Ocean, and their commanders exchanged the first international handshake in space through a specially built docking adapter module. The joint mission conducted five docking and undocking maneuvers and shared four crew transfer sessions over two days.
events.revealBlurb: July 17, 1975 — Apollo–Soyuz. Stafford and Leonov — who had made the first spacewalk a decade earlier — greeted each other in each other's languages. The crews exchanged seeds, flags, and medals. This was the last flight of an Apollo spacecraft and the last US human spaceflight for six years, until STS-1 in 1981.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: Intel Founded
events.blurb: Two former engineers from a Silicon Valley semiconductor firm incorporated a new company — named by combining "integrated" and "electronics" — to build memory chips. They raised $2.5 million in three days by phoning Arthur Rock, a venture capitalist. Their first memory product sold poorly; a side project to build a calculator chip would, three years later, lead them to invent the microprocessor and change the direction of the industry.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1968 — Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce. Their early employees included Andy Grove, later to become Intel's famously paranoid CEO. The name "Intel" had been claimed by a hotel chain; they paid $15,000 for the trademark.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Deep Blue Beats Kasparov
events.blurb: An IBM chess-playing computer, running on a 480-processor supercomputer in New York and evaluating 200 million positions per second, defeated the reigning world chess champion in the sixth game of a six-game match. The loss — the first time a computer had defeated a world champion in a regulation match — the champion afterward accused IBM of cheating by having grandmasters intervene in the machine's moves, which IBM denied. IBM retired the machine immediately after the match.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1997 — Deep Blue vs. Garry Kasparov, New York. Final match score: 3.5–2.5 Deep Blue. The specific "intuition" move that shocked Kasparov (game 2, move 37) was later attributed to a bug in the code forcing a fallback routine.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: Parthenon Completed
events.blurb: A marble temple dedicated to the patron goddess of an Athenian acropolis was completed after fifteen years of work. The structure refined classical Doric proportions, incorporated subtle optical corrections (all its columns lean slightly inward, curved "entasis" swelling their shafts) so the temple appears perfectly rectilinear from a distance, and housed a 12-metre ivory-and-gold statue of Athena. It stood substantially intact for over 2,000 years until a Venetian shell hit a Turkish powder magazine inside it in 1687.
events.revealBlurb: 438 BCE — Ictinus and Callicrates, architects, under Phidias as sculptor. Built on the acropolis of Athens under Pericles. The Elgin Marbles, sold to the British Museum in 1816, are fragments of the Parthenon's sculptural programme — still the subject of Greek repatriation demands.

events.title: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.blurb: An Umayyad caliph completed an octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount of a holy city, sheltering a rock Muslims believe the prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from. Its distinctive gilded dome, 20 metres across, shimmered over the Old City; its interior walls were covered in Byzantine-style mosaics in golden, green, and blue. It is the oldest extant Islamic building and one of the earliest examples of monumental Islamic architecture.
events.revealBlurb: 691 CE — Caliph Abd al-Malik in Jerusalem. Built on the Noble Sanctuary, also the site of the ancient Jewish Second Temple. The gilded dome has been re-gilded many times; the current covering, added in 1993, used 80 kilograms of gold donated by King Hussein of Jordan.

events.title: Machu Picchu Built
events.blurb: An Inca emperor's royal estate was built at 2,430 metres on a narrow mountain ridge above a river in the Andes, with 200 stone buildings — agricultural terraces, palaces, temples — arranged on a mountain site that seemed intended for dramatic rather than practical reasons. It was abandoned roughly a century later for unclear reasons, possibly connected to the Spanish conquest of the Inca. The site remained unknown to the Spanish and, largely, to the outside world until 1911.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1450 — emperor Pachacuti. The American explorer Hiram Bingham encountered it on July 24, 1911. Local farmers had never really forgotten it; the "rediscovery" was primarily for outside audiences. It is now one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
