events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: The Breakfast Club Released
events.blurb: A film about five high-school students from different cliques stuck together for a Saturday detention in the school library opened in American theatres. The cast — a nerd, a jock, a princess, a rebel, a weirdo — talked, argued, and bonded over 97 minutes in a script tight enough that one actor later claimed much of it felt improvised. The film defined a style of introspective teen comedy-drama the decade would become known for. It grossed $45 million on a $1 million budget.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1985 — John Hughes directing Emilio Estevez, Molly Ringwald, Judd Nelson, Ally Sheedy, and Anthony Michael Hall. Hughes had written the script in a single weekend, 1982. The final fist-pump shot, set to Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)," became iconic.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Tamagotchi Released
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company released a small egg-shaped plastic keychain with a tiny LCD screen and three buttons. The device simulated a virtual pet that needed feeding, playing with, and cleaning up after — with beeps demanding attention at all hours, including in the middle of lessons in schools. Schools banned them. 40 million units sold globally. The craze prefigured the attention-hijacking mobile apps of decades later.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 1996 — Bandai. Designed by Akihiro Yokoi and Aki Maita. Later versions could be put to sleep or paused; the original would simply "die" if neglected, and the keychain had to be reset. The name combines Japanese "tamago" (egg) and "watch."

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: Street Fighter II Released in Arcades
events.blurb: Eight distinct fighters, each with their own special moves activated by precise joystick motions, turned a local arcade into a public arena. Players lined their quarters on the cabinet bezel to declare "next game." The fighting game genre was born, arcade revenues spiked, and a competitive meta-game of frame-perfect inputs arose organically.
events.revealBlurb: February–March 1991 — Street Fighter II: The World Warrior released in North American arcades February 6 and in Japan March 7. The SNES port sold 6.3 million copies. The game is credited with single-handedly reviving the arcade industry.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale Mode Launches
events.blurb: Epic released a free-to-play mode in which 100 players parachuted onto an island and fought until one survived, funded entirely by cosmetic purchases. Within two months it had more players than any game in history. It didn't invent the battle royale genre, but it perfected the business model — and convinced the rest of the industry that free-to-play with optional cosmetics was the future.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2017 — Fortnite Battle Royale launched free on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One. Within two months it had 45 million players. The game's in-game concerts — including Travis Scott's 2020 event with 12.3 million simultaneous viewers — redefined live entertainment.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Tangshan Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck a heavily industrialized city in northern China at 3:42 AM, when residents were asleep in masonry buildings that collapsed upon them. Official Chinese figures put the death toll at 242,000, but some estimates exceed 650,000. It is the second-deadliest earthquake of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: July 28, 1976 — Tangshan, Hebei Province. Mao Zedong, dying in Beijing, was briefly informed and reportedly wept. He died six weeks later; many traditional Chinese interpreters saw the quake as the Mandate of Heaven being withdrawn from his regime.

events.title: Nepal Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central Nepal, flattening villages in the mountainous countryside, damaging UNESCO-listed temples in the capital, and triggering avalanches that killed 22 climbers at Mount Everest base camp. The final death toll approached 9,000. Much of the historic royal square in Kathmandu was reduced to rubble.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 2015 — Gorkha district. The quake moved Mount Everest about 3 centimetres southwest and rose Kathmandu by 1 metre. A 16-year-old boy was pulled alive from a collapsed building five days later.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Rosa Parks Arrested
events.blurb: A 42-year-old department-store seamstress and longtime NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat on a city bus in an Alabama capital when the white section filled up and the driver demanded the first row of Black seating. She was arrested for violating municipal segregation ordinances. The local Black community organized a one-day bus boycott that became a 381-day boycott.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1955 — Montgomery, Alabama. Parks was not, as legend has it, "too tired" to move — she was a trained activist who had attended a civil rights training school months earlier. Her act was calculated. A 26-year-old new preacher in town, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the boycott.

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Korean War Armistice
events.blurb: After three years and more than two million deaths, military commanders from three nations signed a ceasefire in a frontier village, establishing a 4-kilometre-wide demilitarized strip along the 38th parallel where fighting had essentially started. No peace treaty has ever been signed. The two Koreas remain technically at war.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1953 — signed at Panmunjom. The DMZ is now the most heavily mined place on Earth. Because no peace treaty followed, a single gunshot across the line could theoretically restart the war tomorrow.

events.title: Kitchen Debate
events.blurb: At the opening of an American National Exhibition in Moscow, a U.S. vice president and a Soviet premier stood beside a model suburban kitchen and argued about consumer goods, nuclear weapons, and the relative virtues of their systems. Live cameras caught every jabbing finger. Polaroid prints of the exchange appeared in American newspapers within days.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1959 — Richard Nixon and Nikita Khrushchev at Sokolniki Park. The kitchen was a General Electric display. Nixon's ability to hold his own in the unscripted shouting match boosted his 1960 presidential prospects (though not quite enough).

events.title: Berlin Wall Built
events.blurb: Overnight, East German soldiers and workers unrolled barbed wire along the jagged frontier between the two halves of a divided city, cutting off the escape route that some 3.5 million people had used to flee west over the previous twelve years. Within days the wire was replaced with concrete. Families woke to find themselves permanently separated from relatives one street away.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1961 — construction began at 2 AM on a Sunday. The wall eventually grew to 155 kilometres, with 302 watchtowers and a "death strip" of raked sand and trip-wires. At least 140 people died trying to cross it going west.

events.title: Gulf of Tonkin Incident
events.blurb: A U.S. Navy destroyer reported it had been attacked by small torpedo boats off the North Vietnamese coast. Two nights later, the same destroyer and a second reported a second attack in bad weather — an attack that likely never happened. Within days, Congress passed a resolution authorizing the president to use "all necessary measures" in Southeast Asia, opening the door to full-scale war.
events.revealBlurb: August 2 and 4, 1964 — the second "attack" was almost certainly radar ghosts and jumpy sonar operators. The resolution passed the House 416-0 and the Senate 88-2. Declassified NSA documents in 2005 confirmed the fabrication.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.blurb: A Roman general of Germanic birth led a coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians, and Alans against a massive Hunnic invasion of Gaul under their formidable king. The battle — one of the largest ever fought in antiquity — ended in an indecisive but bloody Roman-allied victory that stopped the Huns' westward expansion. The Hunnic king would die suddenly two years later on his wedding night from a burst blood vessel; his empire collapsed within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: 451 CE — Flavius Aetius (Roman) and Theodoric I (Visigoth) vs. Attila the Hun. Theodoric was killed in the battle. Attila's death in 453, on his wedding night to a Germanic princess named Ildico, was probably from an esophageal hemorrhage. His sons squabbled; the Hunnic Empire dissolved.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Mughal-e-Azam Released
events.blurb: A Mughal-court epic that took sixteen years to complete — halted twice by financial collapse and partitioned away from its original cast — cost ₹1.5 crore, more than any previous Indian film, and spent ₹1 crore on a single song filmed in a replica of the Sheesh Mahal built with imported Belgian glass. Released in black and white, it was the highest-grossing Indian film for fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1960 — directed by K. Asif. The original Akbar died before filming could restart; the entire cast was rebuilt after Partition. In 2004 it became the first Indian black-and-white film to be digitally colourised and theatrically re-released — and was a commercial success all over again.

events.title: Anand Released
events.blurb: A terminally ill man facing lymphosarcoma of the intestine spends his remaining months arguing that life is worth celebrating — while his doctor-friend records him in a notebook — in a film whose two leads delivered career-defining performances on opposite emotional registers. Its final line, spoken after death, became among the most quoted in Hindi cinema.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1971 — directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, dialogues by Gulzar. Rajesh Khanna was at the absolute peak of his popularity; Amitabh Bachchan was still a supporting player. The film reportedly made Amitabh Bachchan weep on set during the final sequence — which Mukherjee kept in the film.

events.title: Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! Released
events.blurb: A fourteen-song, over-three-hour family wedding drama that critics pre-screened and privately predicted was an unreleasable disaster became, on release, the first Hindi film to gross ₹1 billion — selling 74 million tickets domestically, the highest footfall for any Hindi film since the 1990s. The industry pivoted overnight toward family-oriented, non-violent spectacle.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1994 — director Sooraj Barjatya, a sequel of sorts to his earlier Maine Pyar Kiya. Salman Khan and Madhuri Dixit were cast against type as wholesome leads. The film ran in a Mumbai multiplex for over three years without leaving screens.

events.title: First Website Goes Live
events.blurb: The first webpage to be publicly accessible on the internet was posted from a workstation in a Swiss laboratory. It explained what the World Wide Web was, how to set up a web server, and how to use a web browser. Its URL ended in ".ch"; its creator had built the whole stack — browser, server, editor, protocol — in about a year and a half.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1991 — info.cern.ch, by Tim Berners-Lee. The original page was lost at one point; CERN restored a 1992 copy in 2013. The server, a NeXT workstation, is still on display with a sticker reading "DO NOT POWER DOWN — THIS IS A SERVER."

events.title: ILOVEYOU Virus
events.blurb: A 25 MB computer virus disguised as a love letter attachment from a known correspondent began spreading through Microsoft Outlook email clients at dawn local time in a Southeast Asian capital. Within ten hours it had infected over ten million Windows PCs worldwide, overwriting user documents, image files, and multimedia files with copies of itself. The authors could not be prosecuted because the Philippines at the time had no law against writing malicious software.
events.revealBlurb: May 4-5, 2000 — written by Onel de Guzman, a computer-science dropout in Manila. Damage estimates ranged from $5 billion to $10 billion. The Philippines passed its first cybercrime law in response. De Guzman was unmasked by a journalist 20 years later.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: Banting Discovers Insulin
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Canadian surgeon and a 22-year-old graduate student, working in a borrowed University of Toronto lab through a hot summer, isolated an extract from dog pancreases that, when injected into diabetic dogs, brought their blood sugar back toward normal. By January of the following year, they had injected a 14-year-old boy dying of diabetes; he recovered dramatically. Diabetes, previously a death sentence for type 1 patients, became a manageable chronic disease.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1921 — Frederick Banting and Charles Best. Banting and mentor John Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel; Banting split his prize money with Best. The team sold the patent rights to the University of Toronto for one dollar each. Insulin remains a life-saving medication for tens of millions.

events.title: First Successful Organ Transplant
events.blurb: A Boston surgical team performed the first successful kidney transplant, grafting a kidney donated by a healthy 23-year-old into his identical twin, who had been dying of chronic nephritis. The donor-recipient genetic match avoided rejection in an era before immunosuppressive drugs existed. The recipient lived eight more years; the donor lived another 56. The operation established organ transplantation as a viable medical field.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1954 — Joseph Murray at Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, Boston. Donor: Ronald Herrick. Recipient: Richard Herrick. Murray won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Cyclosporine, the immunosuppressive that would permit non-related transplants, was not discovered until the 1970s.

events.title: First Test-Tube Baby
events.blurb: A baby girl was delivered by caesarean section at a Lancashire hospital — the first human born via in vitro fertilization. Her conception had involved an egg retrieved from her mother, fertilized in a laboratory dish, and implanted in the uterus nine years after the research team had first proposed the technique. The birth prompted intense ethical debate and religious protest. By 2020, about 1 percent of the world's babies were born via IVF.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1978 — Louise Brown at Oldham General Hospital. Pioneers: Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe, Jean Purdy. Edwards won the Nobel Prize in 2010 at age 85; Steptoe and Purdy had died. Brown herself had a second son born naturally in 2013.

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: HPV Vaccine Approved
events.blurb: A quadrivalent vaccine against human papillomavirus — the cause of virtually all cervical cancers and several other cancers — received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration for girls and women aged 9-26. The vaccine, developed initially by an Australian immunologist and colleagues, had been shown in clinical trials to be nearly 100 percent effective at preventing infection by the viral strains responsible for 70 percent of cervical cancer. Cervical cancer incidence began declining visibly within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 2006 — Gardasil (Merck), developed from research by Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou. Australia's school-based vaccination program has since essentially eliminated cervical-cancer-causing HPV strains from young women there. The vaccine's politically fraught rollout in the US slowed uptake in the 2010s.
